paras: The Pecan Grove posse shooting was a gunfight on October 19, 1903, near Pecan Grove plantation in St. Charles Parish, Louisiana, in which a constable's posse killed three Black railroad workers and wounded about seven others. The posse had gone out over charges that some of the men owed unpaid debts, and no member of it was hurt. White papers across the country ran the story as a battle with a band of Black men led by a white man, while the Richmond Planet called it 'another butchery'.

The men were railroad hands working for the Mississippi Valley railroad, which The Sun identified as the Yazoo and Mississippi Valley line, then raising its tracks. They numbered about eighteen and worked under a white man named Pat McGee, spelled 'Migee' in one copy. According to the Associated Press dispatch, a complaint was lodged that some of them had contracted debts and refused to pay, and charges were filed.

Constable Songy, whose name was also printed 'Sonyea' and 'Charles Sorgy', went out to the camp, and on the way John Hinds, described as McGee's assistant, 'covered him with a shotgun and commanded him to keep away from the camp.' The Sun's dispatch placed this on Saturday and said the constable had been trying to serve a legal notice on one of the men. The constable returned to St. Rose and organized a posse, which The Sun described as five other white men, 'well armed and on horseback.'

Near the camp the posse met McGee and the men, whom the wire described as 'all heavily armed.' In the AP version both sides took cover in the high weeds and fought for twenty minutes, until the men 'finally lost their nerve and fled'; The Sun said McGee and the workers fired first as the posse approached. Three men were found dead in the fields, and the wounded, seven in The Sun's count, were cared for at the nearby settlement of Elkinsville.

McGee and the surviving men fled to the swamps, where they were reported to be searched for, and the dispatch warned that 'further trouble' was feared. None of the dead was named in any report, and the coverage includes no inquest, arrest or later court action.

The Associated Press account, datelined New Orleans, October 20, ran on October 20 and 21 in papers from Minneapolis, Butte and Topeka to Savannah, Montgomery and Richmond, usually nearly verbatim. Headlines varied in emphasis: the Savannah Morning News had a posse that 'DEFEATED BAND OF LAWLESS NEGROES', the New-York Tribune said the men would 'Fight Rather Than Pay Debts', and the Paducah Sun headed a garbled version 'A RACE WAR'. The Butte Inter Mountain's headline said the constable was 'Fired Upon From Woods' while serving a warrant, though its text did not say so, and several papers and the Washington Evening Star's weekly summary called the posse a sheriff's posse.

Every white account came from the posse's side, and none reported what the workers said. The only Black-press response found, a Richmond Planet editorial of October 31 titled 'ANOTHER BUTCHERY', retold the same facts but said that 'White men organized under the leadership of a constable and proceeded to kill them.' The Planet objected that 'The newspapers call it a race war instead of a race butchery, as only colored men were killed,' and said a Black man in such conflicts 'should resolve to sell his life as dearly as possible.'

Counts of the wounded differ by copy: seven, 'seven or eight', eight, and 'eighty' in the garbled Paducah version. The Omaha Daily Bee put the band the posse met at eight men rather than eighteen, likely a dropped digit. On who opened fire, The Sun blamed the workers, the AP text did not say, and the Planet held the posse responsible for the killing.

reader.title: Pecan Grove posse shooting
bases: Three Black railroad workers were killed when a constable's posse went to their camp over debt charges and a gunfight followed (A5, A12, A13).

The three men were killed in a reported exchange of fire with a constable's posse sent to act on filed debt charges, and no paper describes the posse as acting outside the law (A5, A13); the only accounts come from the posse's side, and the Richmond Planet called the killings a 'butchery' (A24).

The Associated Press dispatch (A5, A12) and a separate New Orleans dispatch in The Sun (A13), which gives different names and details, agree on three Black men killed and about seven wounded in a fight with a constable's posse at Pecan Grove plantation.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch
accounts.gist: After Hinds turned the constable away with a shotgun, the constable returned with a posse, met eighteen heavily armed men and McGee, and both sides fought from the weeds for twenty minutes until the men 'lost their nerve and fled'.

accounts.label: The Sun's New Orleans dispatch
accounts.gist: Constable Sorgy, driven from the camp while serving a legal notice on Saturday, returned with five mounted white men; McGee and the men fired first as the posse approached.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet editorial
accounts.gist: White men organized under a constable 'proceeded to kill' the workers; it was a butchery, not a race war, since only Black men died.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP text from New Orleans nearly verbatim under headlines like 'THREE KILLED IN A BLOODY FIGHT' and 'BATTLE IN THE WEEDS'.
The Savannah Morning News headlined a posse that 'DEFEATED BAND OF LAWLESS NEGROES', and the New-York Tribune said the men would 'Fight Rather Than Pay Debts'.
The Paducah Sun headlined it 'A RACE WAR', and the Butte Inter Mountain's headline had the constable 'Fired Upon From Woods', a detail its body text did not carry.
The Sun of New York ran a separate dispatch under 'THREE NEGROES KILLED' describing 'a White Posse's Charge on a Railroad Camp'.
The Richmond Planet's editorial 'ANOTHER BUTCHERY' rejected the 'race war' label and urged armed self-defense.

conflicts.note: 'Eighty' appears only in the short Paducah copy, which also garbles the parish name; it is a wire or typesetting error for 'seven or eight'.
The Sun says 'yesterday' in a dispatch dated Oct. 20, and the Planet says Oct. 19; the AP text gives no day.

Black: the three killed and the wounded are described as 'negroes' or 'colored men'; their leader McGee was white.
Pecan Grove plantation, about thirty miles above New Orleans; posse organized at St. Rose; wounded cared for at Elkinsville.
